title: The tungsten-and-black-mass export lock-in: coverage is all about pressuring China, none of it about who the domestic feedstock moat actually helps
thesis: On July 30, 2026 the President issued a Determination under the Defense Production Act naming certain recoverable critical minerals and materials, including tungsten waste and scrap and lithium-ion battery 'black mass', essential to national defense. BIS's resulting Temporary Final Rule (published 2026-08-06, effective 2026-08-27, running at least one year) requires any US person selling these materials to allocate 100% of monthly sales to US persons, absent a BIS exception. Every source found this run frames this as pressure on Chinese recyclers and refiners, which is the correct first-order read: China is the largest buyer of both feedstocks today. What none of that coverage does is name the other side of a supply lock-in, the US and allied recyclers and processors who now hold a full year of guaranteed, price-protected domestic feedstock access. American Battery Technology Company (Nasdaq: ABAT) is a confirmed, listed, currently-operating US black-mass recycler whose own public materials describe shifting its black-mass marketing strategy toward domestic buyers, which is exactly the dynamic this rule creates, but no fetched source this run ties ABAT or any other named recycler to the rule as a beneficiary with a dated quote. Industry reaction is itself split on this point: domestic recyclers support the rule while others worry the US lacks the processing capacity to absorb the locked-in supply, which is precisely the open question a chain build exists to answer.
why_now: The rule is not proposed, it is in force: it took effect 2026-08-27, ten days before this card. It runs for at least one year under DPAS Directive Allocation Order authority, with BIS's public comment period open through 2026-11-04, so the enforcement window and the further-rulemaking window are both live now. The Presidential Determination language itself states the materials are 'scarce' and 'essential to national defense,' which is the same national-security framing that has recurred across this repo's other critical-minerals cards (rare earths) and argues this is a mechanism, not a one-off.
retail_gap: Legal-alert and trade-press coverage (Holland & Knight, Bergeson & Campbell, Baker McKenzie, Mondaq, Recycling Today) is thorough on the rule's mechanics and its pressure on Chinese buyers, and is silent on which specific listed US or allied companies capture the resulting feedstock advantage, and whether any of them have the processing capacity to actually use it. That capacity question is explicitly live: industry reaction is described as mixed, with domestic recyclers supporting the rule while others worry about insufficient domestic capacity and processing capability. Nobody found this run has connected the rule to a specific investable name with a verified, dated claim; ABAT's own domestic-strategy shift is confirmed only by secondary reporting on its public materials, not by a page this run could fetch and quote directly, so it is named here as the clearest candidate for chain-build verification rather than as an established position.

unmappedness.rationale: Scored at 62 because the occurrence itself, a dated, in-force federal rule with a defined one-year window and a stated national-security rationale, is fully public and thoroughly covered by trade and legal press; that caps the score below the mid-70s this card would earn if the rule itself were obscure. Held above 60 because the beneficiary side of the lock-in is genuinely unaddressed: no source fetched this run names a specific listed domestic recycler or tungsten processor as a beneficiary with verified detail, the strongest candidate (ABAT) is confirmed only through unfetched secondary reporting, and the industry's own stated uncertainty about whether US processing capacity can absorb the locked-in feedstock is an open, unscored question rather than a settled fact anywhere found.

evidence.claim: The rule takes effect August 27, 2026 and expires one year later, although BIS may extend the effective time period beyond this date; beginning August 27, 2026, U.S. persons that sell black mass and tungsten waste and scrap must allocate 100 percent of their monthly sales to U.S. persons, unless they first obtain an adjustment or exception from BIS. Black mass is defined as any shredded lithium-ion battery scrap containing cathode material (lithium, cobalt, nickel, manganese), anode material (graphite, silicon), or other residual battery cell materials.
evidence.source_name: Holland & Knight, BIS Imposes Critical Minerals Export Restrictions on Black Mass and Tungsten Waste and Scrap
